concept: Crypto autotrading bot monitor reliability and operations
summary: Source-anchored research for Crypto autotrading bot monitor reliability and operations. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: For Coinbase Exchange level2, size is the replacement quantity at the price level, not a delta, and zero removes a level. Binance also instructs consumers to set the new quantity and remove levels with zero quantity; adding these quantities as increments would violate both contracts. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

A closed-trade drawdown protection is not the same quantity as a daily account loss guard including unrealized losses: Freqtrade documents the former, while Vantixs recommends the latter. Monitoring should name which loss measure each threshold actually governs. (medium confidence)

In Freqtrade, the documented live iteration performs distinct activities, including loading persisted trades, analyzing strategy data, and updating open-order state from the exchange. Treating evidence of one completed activity as evidence of all of them is unsupported; per-stage progress evidence is a monitor design inference from this execution structure. (low confidence)

Google SRE recommends paging for urgent, actionable conditions that are actively or imminently user-visible; frequent low-value pages can cause responders to ignore real incidents. Apply this criterion when deciding which bot events require immediate human attention. (low confidence)

Google’s incident-management model assigns system modifications to the operations team, keeps a live incident document, and requires explicit acknowledgment when incident command changes hands. A bot recovery runbook can use these controls to coordinate responders and preserve continuity. (low confidence)

Google incident guidance prioritizes stopping the damage, restoring service, and preserving evidence for root-cause analysis. It assigns system modifications during an incident to the operations team, which supports a runbook with one coordinated recovery owner. (low confidence)

Freqtrade documents a systemd watchdog that can restart the bot after failures. Its documentation explicitly says the bot-to-systemd notification communication does not work when the bot runs in Docker; deployment-specific recovery mechanisms therefore need separate evaluation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Monitor market-data freshness per symbol and retain both exchange-event and local receive timestamps. EODHD explicitly separates these timestamps and warns that a connected feed can starve individual symbols; Freqtrade incident logs show outdated candles alongside a RUNNING process heartbeat. (medium confidence)

For Kraken book checksum validation, process all price-level updates in a message before calculating the checksum, delete levels with zero qty, truncate to subscribed depth after updates, and preserve price and qty precision with decimal or string decoding. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

For a proposed crypto-bot monitor drill suite, run a synthetic baseline and then repeat the workload with faults such as dependency disconnection, latency, process restart or thread stalls. This adapts fault-injection practices demonstrated by Microsoft and WarpStream; it is a design recommendation, not evidence of an existing bot implementation. (medium confidence)

More aggressive fault injection is not automatically better coverage. FoundationDB tunes fault distributions because excessive fault rates can confine execution to a small state space; monitor drills should therefore include intervals in which useful work and recovery can proceed. The monitor recommendation is an inference. (low confidence)

Kubernetes conditions include observedGeneration to identify the desired-state generation behind an observation; the conventions explicitly describe a condition as out of date when that generation lags the current generation. Bot-monitor adaptation: bind status evidence to the configuration revision it actually observed. (low confidence)

OpenTelemetry supports optional `TraceId` and `SpanId` fields for request and span correlation; if a span identifier is present, a trace identifier should also be present. A bot evidence model can use those fields when the relevant operation has trace context. (low confidence)

Bybit documents two Filled order messages when cancellation races with execution: one reports execution and the other reports the rejected cancellation. A monitor must not count those status messages as two independent fills. (low confidence)

NautilusTrader compares net positions per account and instrument using account quantity tolerance. When a venue reports both long and short positions, startup validation requires both side totals to match; equal net quantity alone is insufficient. Strategy ownership can also be ambiguous when several strategies share an account-level net position. (low confidence)

A 2022 Freqtrade maintainer reply states that the bot only handled its own orders and did not expect to detect a manually closed position. The maintainer could not diagnose the reported rejection without earlier logs. This is historical scope evidence, not proof of current Freqtrade behavior or a confirmed root cause. (low confidence)

NautilusTrader startup validation matches hedging positions by exact venue position identity and quantity, and netting positions by account and instrument within account tolerance. When the venue reports both long and short positions, matching only net quantity is insufficient. (low confidence)

NautilusTrader caps targeted single-order reconciliation queries per cycle, defers remaining orders, and spaces consecutive queries to avoid venue rate limits. This provides a concrete bounded-query pattern for reconciliation after bulk-query failures. (low confidence)

Freqtrade documents `MaxDrawdown` over closed trades in its lookback window. Its default ratios calculation uses cumulative profit ratios; its equity calculation uses starting balance and cumulative absolute profit. The guide warns these can differ when position sizes change. This closed-trade protection should not be presented as a continuously marked unrealized-loss circuit breaker. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Freqtrade documents that changes to `available_capital` require a configuration reload. Reducing it while trades are open does not exit those trades; the difference returns to the wallet when they conclude. This setting replaces `tradable_balance_ratio`. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

The Freqtrade Telegram guide warns that pause/stopentry is not persisted and resets when the bot restarts. A restart must not be assumed to preserve a previously requested pause; the monitor should verify the resulting state. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Kraken recommends renewing its dead-man timer every 15 to 30 seconds with a timeout of 60 seconds. It also recommends disabling the timer before scheduled trading-engine maintenance and warns that an enabled timer will cause order cancellation when the engine returns from downtime. These are vendor recommendations, not universal timing requirements. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

A market-data silence threshold must account for channel semantics (design inference). Coinbase ticker_batch sends every 5000 milliseconds only if there is a change, while Binance specifies 1000ms updates for 1s klines and 2000ms for other kline intervals. Silence alone therefore needs channel-specific interpretation. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

In a first-person bot postmortem, the alert executable was available to interactive shells but absent from the cron environment, so Telegram alerts silently failed for weeks. The author recommends a startup ping to expose notification failure. This is an attributed incident report, not an independently verified loss estimate. (low confidence)

In the January 2025 Telegram connection-error thread, a Freqtrade maintainer said Telegram networking failure does not stop the trading bot from executing trades; the reporter confirmed the bot still worked without messages. Treat notification-channel availability and trading availability as separate incident symptoms. (low confidence)

In Freqtrade issue 7299, the reporter said their timestamp-based probe restarted the container after they manually stopped the bot through Telegram. This historical example shows why a recovery policy should distinguish an intentional stop from a failure before restarting. It does not establish current behavior for every deployment. (low confidence)

In the February 27, 2025 Freqtrade discussion, maintainer xmatthias explains that an old WebSocket value can reflect either a disconnect or no trades on an illiquid pair. Last-update age alone cannot identify the cause of silence. (low confidence)

Deterministic failure replay requires control over nondeterministic inputs, including time, random choices, scheduling and I/O. For a bot monitor, the inferred design is to control these inputs at its dependency boundaries; replaying price records alone does not establish deterministic execution. (medium confidence)

A drill needs a correctness oracle, not merely an absence of crashes. FoundationDB uses workload and local assertions; WarpStream checks message identity and monotonic sequences. Applied to a bot monitor, define expected outcomes and invariant violations before injecting each failure. (medium confidence)

A deterministic simulator still needs controlled substitutes for external dependencies. It cannot by itself establish that the real external integration behaves like its mocks; this limits what a simulated exchange can establish about a live crypto venue. (medium confidence)

Deterministic replay does not guarantee that the same scenario reaches the same failure after changing the binary. In its March 2024 investigation, Cockroach Labs reported instrumentation and code changes could change the terminal state; the investigation ultimately produced a reproducing unit test. The inferred practice is to preserve the failing build and scenario and add a focused regression test for the fix. (medium confidence)

Market-data replay is not proof of realistic execution: HftBacktest states that replay cannot change market data or model market impact, and that some partial-fill scenarios remain unrealistic. Use such replay to exercise monitor behavior under recorded inputs; do not treat its fills as proof of what live orders would do. The monitor-use recommendation is an inference. (low confidence)

Simulation correctness results do not establish production performance or fidelity to every dependency. The FoundationDB paper states its simulator cannot reliably detect performance problems and cannot test dependencies outside its simulation-compatible implementation. Antithesis also requires external dependencies to be controlled. For a monitor, supplement deterministic drills with checks against real dependency behavior. (medium confidence)

A rare failure can require correlated faults and internal transitions that ordinary stress testing misses. Cockroach Labs describes a bug diagnosed using deterministic replay and traces; WarpStream describes a failure plus scheduling race found by its fault-injecting simulator. This supports testing adversarial event orderings for monitor code, without implying a guaranteed bug-detection rate. (medium confidence)

Historical guidance in Freqtrade issue 7299 uses the timestamp of the last bot cycle as progress evidence and compares its age with an acceptable strategy-specific cycle time; the maintainer notes that a slow strategy can take well over one minute. This is guidance from the thread, not a verified contract for every installed release. (low confidence)

Design inference: observe the monitoring transport as a dependency in its own right. Hummingbot documents remote monitoring over asynchronous MQTT channels, and issue 8012 reports repeated bridge reconnect messages that made monitoring and inspection difficult; the issue report does not establish a released fix or a universal strategy failure. (medium confidence)

Do not infer a universal healthy value from condition booleans without each condition’s semantics. Kubernetes notes that some conditions are normally true and others normally false, so a generic condition summary cannot be computed without that knowledge. This scopes any proposed single overall bot health indicator. (low confidence)

In NautilusTrader Polymarket issue 4787, a reporter reproduced a terminal Filled report with filled quantity below original quantity, leaving the local order pending cancellation. A maintainer confirmed the mapping and required a terminal state while preserving the separate dust-underfill rule. This illustrates why quantity agreement alone cannot validate an adapter status mapping. (low confidence)

The probablyprofit README exposes a separate emergency-stop status endpoint and lists kill-switch status and risk-limit configuration among preflight checks. This provides a concrete example of checking the risk gate explicitly before enabling trading; it does not establish implementation correctness. (low confidence)

Bitsgap explains that a stop-market order accepts the available execution price, while a stop-limit can remain unfilled if price gaps beyond its limit. A configured stop trigger therefore does not establish a guaranteed loss cap or completed exit. (low confidence)

Freqtrade requires --enable-protections to include protections in backtesting and hyperopt. Its basics documentation also warns that most live callbacks run per iteration while backtesting calls them at most once per candle, subject to --timeframe-detail; historical simulation alone cannot establish identical live halt timing. (medium confidence)

In Freqtrade, `max_open_trades` bounds the number of open trades, while `max_entry_position_adjustment` separately bounds additional entries into an existing trade. The callback guide documents unlimited adjustment entries by default. A trade-count limit alone therefore does not specify the additional-entry limit. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Freqtrade documents temporary protection locks for a pair or all pairs and rounds lock end times up to the next candle. Its backtesting and hyperopt support requires the `--enable-protections` flag. Operational recommendation: record lock expiry and check that protection evaluation was enabled when assessing risk-control test results. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

For bot notification policy, distinguish suppressed events from quiet delivery and from audible notification. The inspected Freqtrade documentation distinguishes on, silent, and off; Google SRE explains why noisy paging can hide actionable incidents. This supports deliberate severity routing rather than enabling every notification equally. (medium confidence)

A Hyperliquid bot operator reports that the notification executable was available through the interactive shell PATH but absent for cron, and that alerts silently failed. Treat this as an attributed incident report: verify alert delivery under the actual scheduler environment rather than assuming interactive success proves unattended delivery. (low confidence)

Google recommends randomized exponential backoff, per-request retry limits, and a server-wide retry budget, and advises against retrying permanent errors or malformed requests. Applied to bot recovery control requests and notification delivery, this supports bounded retries rather than uncontrolled retry loops; it does not establish that replaying a trading action is safe. (low confidence)

Freshness thresholds should follow the exchange, update frequency, asset and consequence of using a stale value. EODHD explicitly labels its example thresholds as non-universal rather than a general safe timeout. (low confidence)

A REST fallback price must retain its own source and timestamp, and should remain distinguishable from a fresh WebSocket tick. EODHD describes REST fallback as a recovery layer rather than proof that the live stream is healthy. (low confidence)

Freqtrade documents that backtesting simulates only part of its live execution logic and that callback frequency can differ between backtesting and live iterations. A monitor drill should exercise operational behavior directly instead of treating matching backtest output as sufficient verification. (low confidence)

Use a fault matrix that includes process restarts, network partitions, latency and delayed execution, and exercise combinations rather than only isolated failures. This is an inferred monitor-drill pattern: FoundationDB injects these classes of faults, and WarpStream describes a data-loss bug requiring both a failed flush and a rare thread interleaving. (medium confidence)

Define the simulation boundary explicitly: external dependencies must be mocked or otherwise controlled for determinism. WarpStream included clients, control-plane nodes and local storage dependencies in its test topology. Applied to a bot monitor, include controlled dependency responses and failures in the harness rather than assuming a deterministic monitor process controls external services. (medium confidence)

A healthy heartbeat does not prove that the service path works. The Gray Failure paper gives an example where the request handler is stuck while heartbeats remain healthy; Google SRE distinguishes internal instrumentation from tests of externally visible behavior. For bot monitoring, retain both perspectives rather than collapsing them into a heartbeat-only health assertion. (medium confidence)

Freqtrade issue 11957 is an attributed disagreement rather than a confirmed heartbeat-only failure: the reporter alleged stopped processing, while maintainer xmatthias challenged the inference from missing debug messages and closed the issue because the logs did not establish the problem. (low confidence)

Design inference: keep desired operation separate from observed bot status, and expose multiple named health conditions instead of assuming that a single running label describes every behavior. Kubernetes separates desired intent from status and supports multiple conditions; the gray-failure example shows why process-level health can diverge from useful work. (medium confidence)

Design inference: define progress against the work the bot is expected to perform, rather than demanding an arbitrary log message on every heartbeat. Freqtrade documents a repeated loop with candle-scoped work; the disputed issue demonstrates that absence of analysis messages at regular log levels does not establish absence of processing. (medium confidence)

External checks and internal evidence serve complementary purposes: Google SRE says black-box checks expose active symptoms but are poor at predicting imminent problems, whereas white-box instrumentation can expose imminent problems and failures masked by retries. A monitor evidence model should retain the observation method instead of treating these observations as interchangeable. (low confidence)

Reconcile orders, fills, and positions separately: NautilusTrader processes venue order and fill reports before checking positions, while Freqtrade updates exchange order state before verifying existing positions. This supports a monitor that compares execution state with venue exposure rather than treating an open-order list as a position ledger. (medium confidence)

Order status and fill quantity are distinct reconciliation inputs. CCXT describes one order producing multiple fills; Bybit exposes remaining quantity, cumulative executed quantity, and average fill price separately. A monitor should compare executed quantities rather than infer execution volume from status-event counts. (medium confidence)

In NautilusTrader, a missing position report, null quantity, or venue without position publication is not evidence of a flat position. A failed position query causes that venue to be skipped for the cycle rather than interpreting absent reports as flat. (low confidence)

Freqtrade protections can lock one pair or all pairs temporarily; lock end times round up to the next candle. Monitor lock scope and expiry rather than interpreting every protection as an indefinite global halt. (low confidence)

Design inference: test alert delivery from the actual scheduled execution environment and monitor the notification path separately from trading. A first-person bot postmortem reports simultaneous trading and alerting failures, while Google SRE recommends combining internal telemetry with external behavior checks. (medium confidence)

In a September 2024 Freqtrade issue, a user still received entry and exit notifications while commands stopped responding. A maintainer explained that sharing one Telegram bot across two Freqtrade instances can disrupt incoming updates while outgoing notifications still work. Recovery diagnosis therefore needs separate checks for both directions. (low confidence)

Google’s incident-management guidance prioritizes stopping the damage, restoring service, and preserving evidence. It recommends documenting incident procedures in advance. These are appropriate runbook priorities for a bot alert that requires human recovery. (low confidence)

The September 2025 report that Freqtrade Telegram integration was completely broken is disputed: the reporter described silent commands, but the maintainer identified an old, modified installation and reported no errors in a manual test of an up-to-date version. This thread does not establish a universal defect in supported releases. (low confidence)

Operational recommendation: reserve pages for actionable incidents and remove duplicate pages. For routine Freqtrade Telegram traffic, silent delivers a message without sound or vibration, while off suppresses that message type. The recommendation combines Google paging criteria with Freqtrade notification controls. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

A snapshot-plus-stream order book requires an explicit bootstrap boundary: queue stream messages, obtain the snapshot, discard messages already covered by its sequence, and replay later messages. Binance and Coinbase Exchange document this pattern. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

For Binance Spot depth, if incoming `U` is greater than the local update ID plus 1, discard the local order book and restart synchronization. Older updates are ignored; quantities replace levels, and zero quantity removes a level. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Binance warns that a REST depth snapshot covers at most 5000 levels on each side; levels outside the initial snapshot remain unknown until they change. A synchronized local book therefore need not represent every price level. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Treat candle completion separately from candle receipt: Binance kline payloads include start time, close time and x indicating whether the kline is closed. An arriving update can describe the still-open candle. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Coinbase Exchange heartbeat messages arrive every second for subscribed products and include sequence numbers and last trade IDs for detecting missed messages. These are application-level market-feed checks. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Delivery guarantees must be checked per channel: Coinbase Exchange warns that matches messages can be dropped and recommends heartbeat plus REST trade backfill, while its level2 channel documentation guarantees delivery of all updates. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Binance Spot documents planned connection expiry after 24 hours, server ping frames every 20 seconds, disconnection if a pong is not received within a minute, and the requirement to echo the ping payload in the pong. Monitor continuity across these connection lifecycle events. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Hossein Nejati Javaremi describes batching and aggregation as deliberate feed design choices that reduce message volume while adding latency up to a batch interval; clients must not assume each received message is one exchange event. Coinbase Exchange documents a level2 batch feed using the most recent event time in the batch. (medium confidence)

Monitor transport liveness separately from market-data completeness (design inference). Binance documents ping/pong connection checks, while Coinbase supplies heartbeat sequence numbers and last trade IDs to detect missed messages; a healthy connection alone does not establish a complete feed. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Implement order-book integrity checks according to the venue protocol (design inference): Binance prescribes snapshot-plus-buffered-update alignment and gap detection, whereas Kraken documents checksum validation for its book channel. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

For Binance Spot, buffer depth events before obtaining the REST snapshot, align the snapshot lastUpdateId with the buffered U/u range, and rebuild the local order book if U exceeds its update ID plus one. Apply quantities as replacements and remove zero-quantity levels. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Coinbase Exchange warns that matches-channel messages can be dropped. It directs consumers to track the last trade ID through the heartbeat channel and fetch missing trades through REST; heartbeats for subscribed products arrive every second. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Coinbase Exchange explicitly describes level2 as guaranteeing delivery of all updates and starting with a snapshot followed by l2update messages. This is a channel-specific documented guarantee; its matches channel separately warns of dropped messages. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Kraken WebSocket v2 book checksums cover only the top 10 price levels regardless of subscription depth. Kraken makes verification optional and permits checking every update or periodically; the documented checksum does not establish integrity of deeper levels. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Measure event age and local receipt gaps as separate monitor signals (design inference). Binance trade payloads distinguish E event time from T trade time and default timestamp units to milliseconds; Coinbase level2 time records the trading-engine event time. Preserve those meanings and units before comparing timestamps. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Game-day drills can validate monitoring systems and human incident processes together. Microsoft describes coordinated outage simulations with fault injection, and recommends testing first in pre-production, restricting blast radius and retaining a way to end an experiment. (low confidence)

In a historical Freqtrade issue, the reporter described different dry-run and backtest results; a project member proposed resampling and the smaller live data window as the likely explanation, explicitly describing the explanation as an assumption. This is a candidate regression scenario, not a confirmed current defect. (low confidence)

Workload quality limits DST: many executions do not establish broad state-space exploration. Antithesis identifies exploration as a separate technical challenge, and Phil Eaton warns that workload design and the fidelity of mocked failures determine what the tests can expose. (medium confidence)

A recovery drill should restore dependencies to a recoverable condition and assert eventual recovery. FoundationDB explicitly tests this property after failures; this provides a model for a monitor drill that checks recovery after the injected outage ends. (low confidence)

Vary seeds, workloads and configurations, then inspect coverage to find missing scenarios. FoundationDB varies configurations and injection parameters and measures conditional coverage; Antithesis documents repeated seeded simulation and invariant checking. For a monitor, preserve a failing scenario and broaden future runs beyond that single replay. (medium confidence)

Kubernetes conditions provide a transferable pattern for incomplete evidence: condition status can be True, False, or Unknown, and an absent condition is interpreted as Unknown. Condition polarity matters, so a generic all-True summary is not valid without knowing each condition meaning. These are Kubernetes conventions, not a pre-existing crypto-bot standard. (low confidence)

Kubernetes condition records distinguish lastTransitionTime, a programmatic reason, and a human-readable message. A bot monitor can adapt that separation so a current condition carries a transition timestamp, a stable reason category, and explanatory detail. (low confidence)

Preserve event time and collection time separately in evidence. OpenTelemetry `Timestamp` is the source-clock event time and may be missing; `ObservedTimestamp` is the collection-system observation time. These fields do not by themselves establish clock synchronization. (low confidence)

OpenTelemetry supplies a structured evidence vocabulary: Resource describes the emitting source, Attributes describe the specific event, and optional TraceId and SpanId fields associate logs with request processing. A bot-monitor implementation can use these concepts to join observations without assuming every event has trace context. (low confidence)

Design inference: retain evidence history separately from the latest status projection. Kubernetes says historical status information can be lost; OpenTelemetry provides event records with time, source, attributes, and trace context. Neither a latest-status object nor that log schema alone guarantees durable audit retention. (medium confidence)

Model desired configuration separately from observed state. Kubernetes distinguishes desired `spec` from current observed `status`; adopting that separation for a bot monitor is an architectural inference, not a bot product guarantee. (low confidence)

Represent each health condition explicitly, including unknown observations. Kubernetes condition `status` can be `True`, `False`, or `Unknown`, and an absent condition means `Unknown`; applying this to bot monitoring avoids interpreting missing evidence as success. (low confidence)

Attach the configuration generation, last transition time, machine-readable reason, and human-readable message to status evidence. Kubernetes defines `observedGeneration`, `lastTransitionTime`, `reason`, and `message` for these roles; a condition based on an older generation can describe obsolete configuration. (low confidence)

Record evidence provenance and context with distinct fields: OpenTelemetry `Resource` describes the emitting source, `InstrumentationScope` describes the emitting scope, and `Attributes` carries event-specific information. Mapping bot identity and monitor identity onto these roles requires an explicit local convention. (low confidence)

A CCXT RequestTimeout leaves the request outcome unknown. For a createOrder timeout, its manual directs clients to check order history and open/closed orders, then balances if the order is no longer open. Blindly interpreting a timeout as rejection can therefore make a retry unsafe. (low confidence)

In NautilusTrader startup reconciliation, an explicit open or flat position report is authoritative; a missing report or null quantity is not evidence of flatness. The documented guarantee applies only to reports included by configured position and instrument filters. (low confidence)

A REST snapshot arriving after a streamed fill need not describe newer state. NautilusTrader explicitly warns that response arrival time, equal timestamps, or timestamps from different clocks do not establish that a snapshot includes the fill. A lower cumulative fill total must be distinguished from an explicit fill correction. (low confidence)

The reporter of NautilusTrader Derive issue 5355 observed a partial IOC fill arriving after cancellation on crates 0.63.0 with the v2 API. The reporter said position, balance, and PnL appeared correct, but the fill carried reconciliation = true and caused their strategy to pause. Treat this as an attributed historical adapter report, not evidence that every reconciliation fill indicates lost exposure. (low confidence)

Freqtrade issue 12681 reports Binance Futures conditional stop orders that could be created but temporarily could not be fetched or cancelled, leading to multiple conditional orders. The maintainer described orders appearing later and said Freqtrade retained their identities. The report scopes an order-not-found response: it did not prove that those conditional orders never existed. (low confidence)
NautilusTrader defines reconciliation as aligning internal order and position state with venue state; it performs startup recovery and continuous checks for runtime discrepancies. (low confidence)

Cancellation can race with execution. Bybit documents two Filled status messages for one cancel/fill race, and CCXT documents a cancel reaching an already filled order. Treating each terminal-status message as an additional fill would therefore be unsafe. (medium confidence)

Reconcile executed quantity separately from terminal status: CCXT says a canceled order may already be partially filled and exposes filled quantity; Bybit exposes cumulative executed quantity and remaining unexecuted quantity. Cancellation does not imply zero execution. (medium confidence)

A missing open-order record does not establish a final cancellation outcome. NautilusTrader explicitly notes that open-order endpoints omit closed orders and uses a targeted single-order query before terminal not-found resolution; CCXT also documents missing closed-order endpoint support on some exchanges. (medium confidence)

NautilusTrader generates external order events for unrecognized or absent client order IDs. CCXT supports user clientOrderId only where the exchange supports it. Attribution logic must therefore account for venue capability and orders outside its recognized client IDs. (medium confidence)

Entry inhibition can preserve exit management: Freqtrade documents /pause, /stopentry and /stopbuy as refusing new positions while handling open trades; go-trader documents a notional cap that holds new opens while closes and stop-loss management continue. A monitor should distinguish this state from stopping the trader. (medium confidence)

Freqtrade StoplossGuard counts stop-loss trades over a configured lookback, stops trading at trade_limit for stop_duration, and supports pair-specific and futures-side-specific scope through only_per_pair and only_per_side. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Vantixs recommends separate caps for per-symbol position size, combined portfolio exposure, daily loss and peak-to-trough drawdown, plus a volatility circuit breaker. It explicitly distinguishes single-day loss limits from cumulative drawdown and calls for a defined daily reset time. (low confidence)

Vantixs recommends defining the halt response in advance: stop new positions, cancel pending orders, decide whether existing positions are held, reduced or flattened, and require manual acknowledgement before a kill-switch restart. This is an attributed design recommendation, not a universal bot behavior. (low confidence)

The go-trader README documents separate live and paper drawdown peaks and latches, a daily loss guard that holds entries until UTC rollover while allowing closes, and a pooled-wallet portfolio kill switch that a restart does not automatically clear. These are project-specific semantics that a monitor must verify for its deployed bot. (low confidence)

Operational recommendation: track entry pause, stopped trader, forced position exit, and exchange order cancellation as distinct controls. Freqtrade documents separate pause, stop and force-exit commands; Kraken documents a countdown that cancels client orders. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Freqtrade warns that `tradable_balance_ratio` applies to current balance, including funds tied up in trades. It does not preserve a fixed absolute reserve after losses or withdrawals. Monitor the reserve in currency units separately if a fixed reserve is required. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Freqtrade documentation gives conflicting accounts of entry pause: the Telegram guide says paused position adjustments are exit-only, while the strategy-callback guide says `/stopentry` still allows buys on existing trades. These are attributed documentation positions; this research does not establish which behavior an installed version implements. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Kraken documents `CancelAllOrdersAfter` as a timeout that cancels all client orders unless refreshed. A timeout of 0 deactivates it. After expiry and cancellation, the timer remains disabled until the client supplies a new non-zero timeout. Monitoring must distinguish an armed timer from an expired or deliberately disabled timer. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Operational recommendation: expose the active halt scope and deadline. Freqtrade offers `/count`, `/locks` and `/unlock` for trade capacity and pair locks; Kraken returns `currentTime` and `triggerTime`, documenting the latter as the cancellation deadline unless extended or disabled. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

narrative.documentConcept: Crypto bot alerting and incident recovery
narrative.text: This probe covers actionable bot alerts, notification-path failures, and coordinated incident recovery. It combines Google SRE guidance with Freqtrade issue discussions and a first-person bot incident write-up. The claims distinguish sending notifications from receiving commands, notification outages from trading outages, and automatic restart from authorized recovery. Recommendations are identified as design inferences. Historical issue reports remain attributed to their authors; a disputed failure report is preserved with the maintainer’s qualification.

narrative.documentConcept: Crypto bot market-data freshness and stream integrity
narrative.text: Market-data monitoring must check freshness per symbol and preserve exchange and receive times. Process heartbeats do not establish candle freshness. Snapshot-plus-stream order books require sequence-aware bootstrap and gap handling. Delivery guarantees differ by channel, and a recent candle update may still describe an unfinished candle. Silence can reflect an illiquid market as well as a failed stream, so freshness limits need context. REST fallback values should remain identifiable by source and timestamp. These checks establish whether the bot is consuming timely and coherent market data.

narrative.documentConcept: Crypto bot monitor failure drills and deterministic replay
narrative.text: Failure drills deliberately disrupt a workload and check behavior against explicit expectations. Deterministic simulation adds control over time, randomness and scheduling so failures can be reproduced. The evidence supports synthetic fault workloads, invariant checks, coordinated game days and conversion of discovered failures into scenario regression tests. For crypto-bot monitors, these are proposed adaptations of distributed-system testing practice. Trading backtests have narrower execution assumptions and do not alone validate operational behavior. Reproducibility can break after code changes, and mocked exchange dependencies leave a real-integration gap.

narrative.documentConcept: Crypto bot monitor state and evidence model
narrative.text: A bot monitor should distinguish desired operation, observed liveness, and demonstrated work progress. This design inference adapts Kubernetes status conventions and the gray-failure observation gap. Evidence records can preserve event time, observation time, source identity, and correlation context using the OpenTelemetry vocabulary. Missing evidence must remain distinguishable from a confirmed failure. The Freqtrade heartbeat-only report is disputed, and the issue retains both the reporter’s allegation and the maintainer’s challenge instead of establishing a bot defect. These are reusable design patterns and historical reports, not a verified deployment specification.

narrative.documentConcept: Crypto bot order and position reconciliation
narrative.text: Order and position reconciliation compares local execution records with venue orders, fills, and exposure. The evidence distinguishes unknown request outcomes, duplicated status notifications, late fills, inconsistent adapter mappings, and snapshots that predate streamed executions. NautilusTrader documents separate order, fill, and position checks; Freqtrade documents updating exchange order state before position checks. Historical issue reports show why a monitor must preserve order identity, inspect quantities and terminal states, and qualify what a missing order or position report proves. Reconciliation labels and net position agreement alone do not establish that every execution was classified correctly.

narrative.documentConcept: Crypto bot risk limits and halt-state monitoring
narrative.text: Risk-limit monitoring must distinguish entry inhibition, temporary protection locks and broader trading halts. Freqtrade documents pair and side scope, expiry, closed-trade drawdown calculations and continued handling of open trades during entry pauses. Repository examples add explicit kill-switch status, preflight checks and restart latches. Vendor guidance recommends separate exposure, daily-loss, cumulative-drawdown and volatility controls, with a defined response and restart policy. Stop-order execution limitations and simulation timing differences constrain what a configured threshold proves. These findings support checking the specific control and its documented semantics rather than treating a single stopped/running label as sufficient.
